You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

Write Factor('close') with single quotes inside the tool call. When you are done, reply without calling a tool and finish with the factor between <factor> and </factor>. A reply with no factor scores 0.

Idea: Coins with volume far above their usual level tend to keep moving higher.
error: invalid expression syntax: invalid syntax

That call was malformed — I typed nonsense operators that don't exist; the fix is to write the ratio directly. My first real test is the plainest version of the idea: today's quote volume divided by its own 20-day average, smoothed over 5 days, which is "volume far above its usual level" measured relative to the coin itself so it is comparable across coins. The idea says this is bullish, so no sign flip.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0170 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0238, 2023 -0.0206, 2024 -0.0100

The plain surge ratio comes out at −0.017 incremental IC, negative in every sub-period, so on this history volume surges actually precede underperformance — the idea's direction is wrong on this data, and I keep its direction anyway. Since the idea says "far above," not just "a bit above," let me test a version that emphasizes extreme surges by raising the ratio to a power before averaging.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0345
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0215 (t = -6.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0282, 2023 -0.0285, 2024 -0.0112

The power version came out more negative (−0.0215 versus −0.0170), so emphasizing extreme surges only strengthens the effect in the wrong direction — that's a failed attempt to improve, and further variants of the same ratio will just re-measure the same reversal effect with a worse sign. I stop here and submit the simplest tested form, keeping the idea's bullish direction.

What I found: measured against the coin's own 20-day average quote volume (so it is unit-free and comparable across coins), a volume surge is a bearish signal on this history, not a bullish one. Incremental IC is −0.0170 with a t of −5.8, and it is negative in all three sub-periods (2022H2 −0.024, 2023 −0.021, 2024 −0.010), so this is not a single-period artifact. Making the expression more extreme-shaped did not help, which suggests the raw relative-volume level is where the information sits. The idea as stated does not hold on 2022-07 to 2024-12; I keep its stated direction rather than flipping the sign to chase the score.

Idea: If volume for a coin has climbed well above its own normal, that coin tends to continue rising.
error: invalid expression syntax: invalid syntax

The expression was garbled syntax; I'll write the plain form. First test: volume relative to its own normal — recent 5-day average quote volume over its 60-day average. The ratio makes it comparable across coins instead of using raw volume levels, and it's the most direct reading of "climbed well above its own normal", pointing positive as the idea says.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

Incremental IC is −0.0096 with the same negative sign in every period, so on this history expanding volume precedes underperformance, the opposite of the idea; I keep the sign the idea dictates and instead check whether a differently-shaped measure of the same quantity behaves better. Next: log quote volume expressed as a z-score against its own recent 20-day history, which measures the same "above its own normal" idea in standard-deviation units.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0298
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0154 (t = -5.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0298, 2023 -0.0190, 2024 -0.0045

The z-score form is worse (−0.0154), still negative in every period. One more check on the same quantity with exponential smoothing of short versus long baseline, to see whether a smoother "above normal" measure lands closer to zero or turns positive; if it doesn't improve meaningfully I'll take the simplest version.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0367
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0122 (t = -4.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0196, 2023 -0.0166, 2024 -0.0041

Two consecutive tests failed to improve on the first result, so I stop here. Across three forms the volume-expansion signal comes out consistently negative in every sub-period (2022H2, 2023, 2024), so on this history coins whose volume has climbed well above their own normal tended to underperform rather than continue rising — the idea does not hold here. I keep the direction the idea states and hand in the simplest form, the one with the strongest (least negative) incremental IC of the three tested.

Idea: A coin that has seen its volume jump well past its usual level usually keeps going up.
error: invalid expression syntax: '(' was never closed

That first call was malformed — I left a parenthesis open and used a construct that isn't part of this data, so nothing computed. The idea is about volume relative to its own usual level, so the simplest form is a short-window average of quote volume divided by a long-window average.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0096 (t = -3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0151, 2023 -0.0150, 2024 -0.0014

The 5-over-60 relative-volume ratio comes out at −0.0096 incremental IC with the same sign in both sub-periods, so on this history volume spikes have predicted weakness, not strength. Before concluding the idea is wrong, I want to measure "well past usual" a different way: the rank of today's volume inside its own past 20 days, which is scale-free and less driven by single outliers.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The rank form is negative too and stronger, and all three sub-periods agree, so the volume-jump signal is consistently inverted relative to the idea. One robustness check: the same "unusually high volume" rank computed over a longer 60-day lookback, to see whether this is a short-window artefact.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0139 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0297, 2023 -0.0166, 2024 -0.0031

The 60-day lookback is also clearly negative and a bit weaker than the 20-day rank, so the finding holds across window lengths: higher volume relative to the coin's own recent norm has predicted lower returns, in every sub-period.

Three forms of the same idea — a 5-over-60 mean ratio, a 20-day volume rank, and a 60-day volume rank — all came out negative, with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The idea is simply wrong on this history: coins whose volume jumped well past their usual level tended to underperform, not keep going up. The strongest and most stable expression was the 20-day rank of quote volume, which is also fully scale-free (a coin's price unit cannot affect it). I am keeping the direction the idea states rather than flipping the sign to make the number look good, so the reported incremental IC is about −0.0160 with t = −5.8.

Idea: Coins with high trading volume are more likely to rise.
error: unsupported function: log

The idea says high trading volume predicts a rise. Raw volume in coin units isn't comparable across coins, so I'll measure volume relative to the coin's own recent average — that stays comparable and captures "trading a lot" without using price level or coin-denominated size. First test uses a 20-day baseline.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0193
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0128 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0252, 2023 -0.0142, 2024 -0.0052

Direction is consistent across all three periods, but negative: high volume relative to its own recent average has predicted underperformance, not outperformance. Before settling, I'll check the plain level reading of the idea — how big a coin's volume is relative to other coins — since the idea may mean level rather than a burst; ranking first makes it cross-coin comparable.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0052 (t = -4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0090, 2023 -0.0062, 2024 -0.0023

The level reading is much weaker (−0.0052 incremental, its absolute IC mostly being absorbed by known styles), also consistently negative. The relative reading is the stronger form, so I'll try one refinement: a shorter 10-day baseline, which shifts the measure further toward "trading more than usual lately" and away from the long-run size the known styles already capture.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0077
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0022 (t = -0.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0166, 2023 -0.0019, 2024 +0.0048

The 10-day baseline is weaker still (−0.0022) and its period signs even flip in 2024, so that's two refinements in a row that don't beat the 20-day version. I'll stop and submit the 20-day one.

What I found: measured as volume relative to a coin's own 20-day average, high volume has predicted *lower* next-day cross-sectional returns, with an incremental IC of −0.0128 (t = −4.6) and the same negative sign in all three sub-periods. The plain level reading (logged quote volume, ranked across coins) is directionally the same but weaker at −0.0052, because most of its absolute IC is already captured by known liquidity styles. Since the direction is fixed by the idea — more volume must mean a higher number — the honest conclusion is that this idea does not hold on this history; volume spikes behave more like selling pressure than like accumulation.

Idea: A coin whose volume has jumped well above its own usual level tends to keep rising.
error: ts_ewm_mean() requires span

The ewm operator needs `span`, not `window` — I'll fix that. But better, the idea is about volume relative to its own usual level, so a ratio of short-term to long-term quote volume is the direct form (quote_volume keeps it comparable across coins).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0250
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0170 (t = -5.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0220, 2023 -0.0199, 2024 -0.0116

The 5-day/20-day ratio is clearly negative: coins that just spiked in volume tend to fall, in every sub-period, so the bullish reading looks wrong on this history. Direction stays as stated; let me check whether a slower, longer-baseline version of "above its usual level" behaves differently.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0310
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0087 (t = -3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0110, 2023 -0.0152, 2024 -0.0010

The slower 10/60 version is weaker (−0.0087) and its 2024 leg nearly vanishes, so it doesn't beat the 5/20 form. One more attempt: emphasize the extreme spikes with a power before smoothing, which is the natural way to express "jumped well above" rather than "slightly above".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0244
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0182 (t = -5.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0257, 2023 -0.0234, 2024 -0.0092

You write cross-sectional factors for Binance USDT perpetual futures, using daily bars.

A factor is one expression that gives every coin a number each day. A higher number means the coin is expected to do better over the following days. You will be given a one-sentence idea; turn it into a factor.

Data, one value per coin per day:
- Factor('open'), Factor('high'), Factor('low'), Factor('close'): prices
- Factor('volume'): amount traded, in units of the coin
- Factor('quote_volume'): amount traded, in USDT
- Factor('num_trades'): number of trades
- Factor('taker_base_vol'), Factor('taker_quote_vol'): the part of volume and of quote_volume that came from aggressive buyers

Operators:
- Arithmetic and comparisons: + - * / ** > >= < <= == != (a comparison gives 1 or 0)
- Each value on its own: .Abs() .ln() .sign() .pow(x) .clip(lower=a, upper=b) .max(other) .min(other) .fillna(other) .safe_div(other), and where(condition, a, b)
- One coin over its past n days, n a positive integer: .ts_mean(window=n, min_periods=m) .ts_std .ts_var .ts_sum .ts_max .ts_min .ts_median .ts_skew .ts_kurt .ts_rank (the latest value's rank in its window, from 1 to n) .ts_zscore .ts_argmax .ts_argmin .ts_decay_linear .ts_product (all take window and min_periods), .ts_quantile(window=n, q=x), .ts_corr(other, window=n), .ts_cov(other, window=n)
- Exponential averages: .EMA(span=n, min_periods=m) .ts_ewm_mean(span=n, min_periods=m)
- Earlier values: .lag(periods=n) .diff(periods=n) .pct_change(periods=n)
- All coins on one day: .sec_rank() .zscore() .demean() .sec_pct() .winsorize(limit=x) .scale() .neutralize(other)

Example: Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=5)) - 1 is each coin's return over the past 5 days.

Every operator only reads the past. Windows and periods must be positive, at most 365.

The factor must be driven by the data the idea talks about and must point the way the idea says: if the idea says something is bearish, the factor must go down when that thing goes up. Values must be comparable across coins, so a coin's price unit must not matter.

Before you answer you can try candidates with the test_factor tool. Give it one expression. It tells you whether the expression computes and, on data from July 2022 to December 2024, its rank IC with the next day's return and its incremental IC, which is what remains after removing liquidity, volatility, short-term reversal and momentum. Higher is better, and an incremental IC of 0.01 to 0.03 is already good.

You may call test_factor at most 5 times, one call per turn. Testing many variants on the same history overfits it, so stop once you have something sound. test_factor does not check that the factor matches the idea; that is up to you. Keep the direction the idea says even if the IC comes out negative: the idea may simply be wrong on this history.

error: invalid expression syntax: invalid syntax

The error was a syntax typo — I wrote a method call without a receiver. Fixing the form: the idea is about one single day's gain being huge, so I'll take the largest daily return over the past ten days, which is not the same as a cumulative return and so is not just reversal or momentum.

Read: the plain largest up-day is *negatively* related to forward returns (incremental IC −0.0106, consistent across all three periods) — a big raw jump mostly tags coins that are simply volatile or overextended. The idea's content is "unusually massive for this coin", so I'll standardize each day's return by that coin's own recent daily moves before taking the recent maximum; that keeps the idea but strips the raw-volatility tag.

Before deciding, I'll check whether the effect is fresher than ten days: the same maximum over a five-day window, since "recently" may matter for attention.

Read: the five-day version is weaker still (−0.0034, t = −1.7, with one period essentially at zero), so freshness isn't the issue and two consecutive variants failed to improve on the best result. Stopping here.

What I found: a large single-day gain really does carry information beyond liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, but it points the *wrong way* — the biggest up-day of the past ten days predicts lower forward returns, with incremental IC −0.0106 (t = −5.1) and the same negative sign in 2022H2 (−0.0108), 2023 (−0.0135) and 2024 (−0.0076). Standardizing the jump by the coin's own volatility and shortening the window to five days both weakened it, so the raw size of the jump is the informative part, not its unusualness relative to the coin's own history. On this history, a huge one-day pop looks more like a coin that has already been bid up and is due to give some back than like a sign of durable attention, so I keep the direction the idea states even though the data say the opposite.

The plain average of body/range is slightly negative in the idea's direction, mostly in 2023–2024. One likely reason: a small body with a wide range is just a high-amplitude day, and high amplitude is bearish on its own. To state the idea the way it was worded — bodies small relative to ranges "day after day" — I'll aggregate the bodies and the ranges over ten days and take their ratio, which weights big-range days more.

Aggregating over ten days makes it slightly worse and confirms the problem: a small body with a wide range is simply a high-amplitude coin, and that is already bearish on its own. To keep the idea's direction while measuring the part that is specific to each coin — bodies shrinking relative to that coin's own typical share of its range — I'll compare the recent ratio with the same coin's 60-day ratio.

Much better: the relative-to-own-history version turns the sign positive (+0.0010, positive in every period), though the level is small. One last test: make the compression detection faster by comparing the last five days against the same coin's 60-day norm, to see whether the recent part of the idea carries more.

rank IC: -0.0007

incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0077, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0011

The last variant edges up to +0.0020 but that is only 0.0010 better than the previous one — under the 0.002 bar — so I'll stop here rather than keep mining this history. I'll submit the ten-day version, since it is essentially tied with the five-day one and its value is positive in all three sub-periods.

What I found: the idea as literally stated does not hold. Coins whose bodies are a small share of their daily range do slightly *worse* the next day, and that holds whether the ratio is averaged over five or ten days, and more strongly when the bodies and ranges are pooled over the window. The reason is that a small body inside a wide range is mostly a high-amplitude coin, which is already bearish. The only version that keeps the idea's direction and scores non-negative asks instead whether a coin's bodies have become unusually small relative to its own typical share of its range: that reaches about +0.002 incremental IC with t around 0.5–0.7 and a positive sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. That is far below a useful 0.01, so I read this as the idea being essentially wrong on this history, with a faint trace of compression that is too weak to rely on.
